edges.effect_quant: A 2024 meta-analysis of adult placebo-controlled trials found that glutamine supplementation improved established gut-permeability markers overall, and earlier surgical and critical-care meta-analyses also pointed toward lower permeability and inflammatory marker burden with glutamine-enriched feeding. The signal is not universal across every acute-care setting, but the direction is consistently toward barrier support rather than barrier injury.
edges.population: adults receiving oral or enteral glutamine supplementation in permeability, surgical, or critical-care clinical trials
edges.mechanism: Glutamine is a preferred fuel for enterocytes and may reduce intestinal permeability by supporting tight-junction integrity, mucosal repair, and epithelial energy supply during physiologic stress. Its clearest role seems to be barrier maintenance under inflammatory or catabolic pressure rather than broad performance supplementation in otherwise healthy adults.
edges.summary: Glutamine supplementation generally appears to improve intestinal permeability markers in adults, especially when the gut barrier is stressed by surgery, critical illness, or other catabolic states. The most up-to-date meta-analysis supports a protective effect, and earlier pooled clinical data point in the same direction, though the signal is stronger for barrier endpoints than for broad clinical outcomes in every population.
edges.caveats: Most supportive studies come from stressed or ill populations rather than healthy community adults, so this edge should not be overgeneralized into a universal gut-health claim. Better barrier markers do not always guarantee shorter hospital stays or lower mortality, and formulation, route, and baseline illness severity likely matter.

evidence.notes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical trials on the effects of glutamine supplementation on gut permeability in adults.

evidence.citation: Liu et al 2016 Exp Ther Med
